reviewBoundary: Four complete CET banks and one complete C1 formation. Fictional search/listening cases and qualified general material/measurement explanations. Same-author all-word/variant review; no independent calibration.

units.title: The pencil that grew shorter
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: The pencil that grew shorter
materials.text:
A wooden pencil looks like a simple object, but its familiar form connects several different materials. The dark mark comes from a core that commonly combines graphite with clay. The wood around that core provides ____1____, making the thin marking material easier to hold and less likely to break in ordinary use.

As a pencil is sharpened, some wood and core are ____2____ to expose a usable point. The pencil gradually becomes shorter. A sharpener does not put the lost material back; it creates a new working end by taking material away.

Pencils are sold in different ____3____, which describe properties of the core rather than the colour of the outer paint. A softer core generally produces a darker mark and wears down more ____4____. The exact result also depends on the paper and the pressure applied by the writer.

The mark can often be ____5____ with an eraser because the material sits on the paper's surface rather than behaving exactly like a liquid ink. That does not mean every mark disappears completely. Heavy ____6____ may leave an indentation, and rough rubbing can damage the sheet.

For someone choosing a pencil, the intended ____7____ matters. A light construction line in a drawing may need a different mark from a bold sketch. There is no reason to assume that one grade is ____8____ for every task.

Even a familiar tool benefits from attention to its limits. A broken point does not prove the entire pencil is useless, while sharpening it without need simply ____9____ material. Understanding how it works can help a user choose and care for it more ____10____. The object remains ordinary, but the decisions behind using it become easier to explain.

questions.explanation: Support names the wood’s physical help for the core. Grades/purpose/ownership/pressure do not name that protective structure.
Shaved means cut off in thin pieces during sharpening. Erased concerns a mark on paper, not exposing the pencil core. Other entries do not describe that removal action.
Grades are core classifications. Pressure/purpose/support are not plural product classes; ownership does not classify hardness.
Quickly matches faster wear of a softer core. Rarely concerns frequency rather than the stated comparative wear process; effectively does not express speed.
Erased directly names removing a mark with an eraser. Shaved concerns cutting the pencil and the other options do not name clearing a mark.
Pressure explains an indentation caused by force. Ownership/purpose/support do not name force applied to the paper.
Purpose names the intended use. Pressure is force, ownership possession and support structure, not the task sought.
Ideal means best suited for a task. Portable concerns carrying, not universal suitability; other words have the wrong grammatical role.
Wastes means consumes material unnecessarily. Collects would gather material and disagree does not take material in this sense.
Effectively describes successful use/care. Quickly concerns speed and rarely frequency, neither the benefit of understanding the tool here.

units.title: Finding an article again
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: Finding an article again
materials.text:
A student remembered reading a useful article but could not find it again. Searching the whole web for one common word produced thousands of ____1____. Most had no connection with the topic she remembered, and the large number made the search harder rather than better.

She began by writing down the ____2____ she could recall: a phrase from the title, the subject and the approximate month. None was certain, so she kept the notes separate from facts she had already checked.

Next she used a search tool's date ____3____ to limit the period. The article might have been older than she thought, so she treated that limit as a starting point, not a guarantee. When no likely result appeared, she could ____4____ the period again.

A quoted phrase can narrow a search, but only if the remembered wording is ____5____. One wrong word may exclude the desired page. She therefore tried both the exact phrase and a version with fewer fixed words.

When she found a promising page, she checked the author's name and the publication ____6____. A copied paragraph on another site was not necessarily the version she had read. She followed the available reference towards the ____7____ source.

Finally, she saved the page address with a short ____8____ explaining why it mattered to her assignment. The note would help her recognise the page later, while the address would make it easier to ____9____.

The search had become more successful because she changed her method, not because she typed the same word faster. Useful searching involves testing a remembered clue, examining what appears and adjusting the next step. Recording the result ____10____ reduces the chance of repeating the entire process tomorrow. It does not guarantee that a website will remain available forever, but it gives a future search a much clearer starting point.

questions.explanation: Results are the returned pages. Details are recalled clues; other nouns do not name the plural search output.
Details are the remembered phrase/topic/month. Results are returned pages, not memories; filter/date/note are single specific things rather than the list of clues.
A date filter limits the period. Date date is not the intended tool term and appetite/note/results do not name that control.
Widen expands the unsuccessful date range. Narrow would reduce it further; decorate/locate do not describe changing range.
Accurate wording makes an exact phrase useful. Original concerns origin and fragile vulnerability, not correspondence to the actual words.
Publication date is checked alongside author. Filter/note/appetite do not name when publication occurred.
Original contrasts the source with a copied paragraph. Accurate is truthfulness, fragile vulnerability, not source priority.
Note names the explanatory saved text. Date is when, filter a control and results returned pages; none names the purpose annotation.
Locate means find the page again. Widen/narrow change a range and decorate alters appearance, not retrieval.
Carefully matches a useful record of address and explanation. Casually weakens the stated care; no other bank adverb supplies that meaning.

units.title: Numbers with units attached
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: Numbers with units attached
materials.text:
A measurement expressed as a bare number is often incomplete. Saying that a board is twenty long leaves the reader without a ____1____. Twenty centimetres and twenty metres describe very different objects, even though the numerical part is identical.

Units provide a shared way to express a quantity, but consistency still requires attention. A table may list values in millimetres while a drawing uses metres. Before combining them, the quantities must be ____2____ into compatible forms. Changing the label alone does not perform the conversion.

The ____3____ of an instrument matters too. A ruler marked only in centimetres does not justify writing a length to many decimal places merely because a calculator can display them. More printed digits do not automatically create greater ____4____ about what was measured.

Repeated measurements can reveal variation, yet repetition does not remove every possible error. An instrument with a shifted zero may give similar readings that are all ____5____ in the same direction. Agreement between repeated readings is therefore different from agreement with an appropriate reference.

Good records preserve the method as well as the final value. They state the instrument, the conditions and any relevant ____6____. When an approximation is used, its role should be visible so that another person can judge whether it is suitable for a new purpose.

This is particularly important when a result is ____7____ from a small trial to a larger design. An assumption acceptable for a rough classroom model may be inadequate for a structure in public use. Similar-looking arithmetic does not make the responsibilities ____8____.

The point is not to bury every number beneath an endless warning. It is to make the information needed for interpretation ____9____. A well-described measurement can support a decision precisely because its limits are known. Treating units, methods and uncertainty as part of the result makes numerical communication more ____10____, while leaving room to improve the measurement when the decision requires it.

questions.explanation: Unit specifies the scale of twenty. Resolution is instrument discrimination, certainty confidence, appetite irrelevant; none supplies centimetres/metres.
Converted means expressed in compatible units. Decorated/celebrated change appearance or status; transferred changes use rather than units.
Resolution is the smallest distinguishable increment. Unit is scale and certainty confidence, not the instrument’s graduation detail.
Certainty names warranted confidence in the measurement. Resolution belongs to the instrument, assumptions premises and appetite a desire.
Biased readings systematically shift in one direction. Absolute/identical concern other properties, not the offset identified.
Assumptions are conditions taken as given in a model. Resolution/unit/certainty do not name those premises.
Transferred means taken into a different-scale application. Converted concerns units; celebrated/decorated do not describe moving the result’s use.
Identical means the same; the text denies equal responsibilities at different stakes. Confidential concerns access and absolute lack of qualification.
Accessible means available to readers for interpretation. Confidential would restrict the needed information; identical/absolute do not address findability.
Responsible communication makes relevant limits known. Celebrated is praise and decorated ornamentation; other entries do not describe this duty.

units.title: What a shaded surface tells us
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: What a shaded surface tells us
materials.text:
On a sunny day, two nearby paving stones may feel very different if one is shaded. The observation invites a ____1____: does the shade explain the difference, or do the stones also differ in material, moisture and earlier exposure?

A useful comparison tries to keep relevant factors ____2____ while changing the one being examined. In practice, outdoor conditions are difficult to control completely. Clouds move, wind changes and shade shifts as the sun's position changes. Recording these conditions helps make the comparison ____3____.

Surface temperature is not the same quantity as air temperature. An instrument aimed at a pavement may describe that ____4____, not the air a person breathes. A report that calls both simply temperature can conceal an important distinction.

There are also different ways to describe human comfort. Air movement, humidity and radiant heat can all contribute. A single surface reading cannot be assumed to ____5____ every aspect of how a place feels. This does not make the reading useless; it defines the question it can help answer.

Timing matters as well. A measurement taken at noon is a ____6____ of one moment, not necessarily a description of the whole afternoon. Repeated observations may reveal a pattern, provided that the method remains sufficiently consistent for the readings to be compared.

For a school project, the aim might be to explain why a shaded seating area seems more inviting. For a planning decision, additional evidence and professional ____7____ may be needed. The amount and kind of evidence should be appropriate to the decision's ____8____, rather than chosen only for convenience.

A convincing account keeps the observation, the proposed explanation and the broader recommendation ____9____. It can connect them without treating them as interchangeable. The small contrast between two stones then becomes an opportunity to think more ____10____ about what is measured and what is inferred. Better questions do not remove the value of an everyday observation; they make its contribution clearer.

questions.explanation: Question introduces alternative explanations. Snapshot is one observation, surface an object and costume irrelevant; none names the inquiry.
Constant means held unchanged for comparison. Permanent is lasting forever rather than controlled during a trial; distinct means separate, not held equal.
Interpretable means capable of being understood in context. Edible/permanent/distinct do not name that methodological benefit.
Surface refers to the pavement being measured. Snapshot names the time slice, not the physical target; expertise/question are not targets.
Capture means represent the full range of comfort. Entertain does not mean measure those aspects; the other choices do not complete that base-verb role.
Snapshot is a reading at one moment. Question/consequences/expertise are not time-limited observations.
Expertise names professional knowledge required for a higher-stakes decision. Costume/surface/snapshot do not name trained judgment.
Consequences are the stakes of the decision. Expertise is capability, surface an object and question inquiry; none names the resulting effects.
Distinct keeps observation/explanation/recommendation conceptually separate. Constant means unchanged and permanent lasting; neither expresses non-interchangeability.
Critically means examining measurement and inference. Privately concerns audience rather than careful evaluation; other entries do not have the needed adverb role.

units.title: Two performances of one tune
units.instruction: Use the word in brackets to form one word that fits each gap.

materials.title: Two performances of one tune
materials.text:
A music club played two recordings of the same short tune without showing the performers' names. The first listening left some ____1____ (CERTAIN) about which version members preferred. Several members said they did not yet know which they preferred.

On the second listening, one student smiled in ____2____ (RECOGNISE): the tune had been used at a family celebration. Her preference was connected with that memory, although the recordings themselves were new to her.

Another listener noticed an ____3____ (EXPECT) pause before the final phrase. He had thought the melody would continue directly, and the interruption made him attend more closely. For someone else, the same pause seemed distracting.

Their different degrees of ____4____ (FAMILIAR) with the tune helped explain some reactions, but not all. Several ____5____ (INTERPRET) were possible, and members pointed to specific moments rather than only saying good or bad.

They discussed the difference between ____6____ (EXPRESS) playing and merely changing speed. A slower phrase could have a purpose, but slowness alone did not settle its effect.

Finally, they judged the versions ____7____ (DEPEND), writing separately before seeing anyone else's choice. Two members still reached incompatible conclusions. Their incompatible verdicts constituted a ____8____ (AGREE), but the exercise had not failed: each could explain the features behind a preference.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with one word formed from CERTAIN.
questions.explanation: The remaining uncertainty is an unknown state; certain is adjective and certainly adverb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with one word formed from RECOGNISE.
questions.explanation: In recognition names identifying the familiar melody and requires the noun recognition. Recognise is verb and recognizable adjective; unlisted variants remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with one word formed from EXPECT.
questions.explanation: An unexpected pause was not anticipated. Expectedly is adverb and expect verb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with one word formed from FAMILIAR.
questions.explanation: Familiarity with the tune requires a noun. Familiar is adjective and familiarly adverb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with one word formed from INTERPRET.
questions.explanation: Several requires plural interpretations. Singular and verb do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with one word formed from EXPRESS.
questions.explanation: Expressive playing uses an adjective. Expression is noun and expressively adverb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with one word formed from DEPEND.
questions.explanation: Independently modifies judged; the context explicitly contrasts separate judgments with copying. Adjective/noun do not modify the verb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with one word formed from AGREE.
questions.explanation: The two incompatible final judgments constitute disagreement. Agreement contradicts the stated difference and agree is verb.
